reuse.why: The change reuses getApproxNumberThreshold and shares the new calculation across five consumers, but introduces expectedScheduleAmount alongside the existing getScheduledAmount abstraction.

duplication.why: Range and approximate calculations are centralized for migrated consumers, but schedule amount dispatch remains parallel to getScheduledAmount and missing-to-zero handling is repeated across callers.

placement.why: API mapping and response types stay in their existing layers, but schedule expectation policy is added to shared/rules.ts despite shared/schedules.ts already owning scheduled amount calculation.

scope.why: The implementation, types, tests, and release notes are focused on schedule amount expectations and the API field.

maintainability.why: The new helper is straightforward, but maintaining competing schedule amount definitions and caller-owned missing-value handling leaves multiple places to update future policy.

bypasses_abstraction.where: expectedScheduleAmount in shared/rules.ts and its five consumers establish a parallel path instead of extending getScheduledAmount in shared/schedules.ts.

disguised_duplication.where: expectedScheduleAmount reshapes getScheduledAmount's number-versus-range dispatch under a new name, while API getExpectedAmount and the two schedules/app.ts callers repeat its existing missing-to-zero policy.

abstraction_drift.where: The evolving expectation helper gains the amount operator and an isapprox branch; API mapping, budget templates, forecast normalization, action synchronization, and transaction posting use this parallel abstraction while getScheduledAmount and preview calculation remain separate.
